headline: Niantic fleet says it plain: fluke deep, sea bass steady, bass biting after dark
subhead: Soft neap currents kept things quiet through Black Point and Twotree, but the tide's about to get its legs back.
body_markdown:
I was leaning on the counter at the tackle shop Tuesday morning listening to one of the Niantic drift boat mates gripe about the current, and he said something that stuck with me: "Water's warm enough to swim in, current's dead enough to nap in." That's about the most honest summary of the last week I've heard. The neap tide phase really did flatten things out through Black Point and Twotree Island Channel, and the fleet felt it — not a bad week, just a soft one, and soft weeks make you work for every fish.

Water's running warm out here. New London's reading 77.4°F, which is a good five degrees above where Western Sound sits right now, and that gradient matters. It's pushed the fluke off the shallow flats in Niantic Bay and onto deeper structure where the bottom stays workable — 30 to 40 feet in Twotree Island Channel and along the edges of the Black Point reef complex. The drift boats that adjusted depth early in the week did fine; the ones that kept working the shallower drifts inside the bay got picked apart by shorts. Bucktail and Gulp combos are still the ticket — white 5-inch Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow on the drift, tipped with a strip of squid when the current's light like it's been. Keeper fluke to 22 inches have come off those deeper channel drifts on the last two hours of the outgoing, when there's at least a little push to work with.

Sea bass and porgies have been the honest fallback all week, and I mean that as a compliment, not a knock. Hole-in-the-Wall and the rock piles off Black Point are holding fish tight to structure, and with the current soft, that's exactly where you want to be — sea bass don't need a screaming tide, they need bait sitting still enough for them to find it. Green crab and squid strips on standard sea bass rigs, 4 to 6 ounces of lead depending on drift speed, straight down into the structure. Porgies have been mixed in on the same spots, plenty of them in the 10 to 12 inch range, keeping rods bent even on the slow days. We flagged this exact pattern a few days back — said to expect steady bottom fishing through this transitional stretch with just light adjustments to presentation, and that's precisely what's played out. Nothing flashy, just dependable.

Striper fishing has gone almost entirely nocturnal, which tracks with what you'd expect once surface water sits in the mid-to-upper 70s. Daytime trips around McCook Point and the mouth of the Niantic River have been mostly quiet, but guys working bunker schools after dark — snag-and-drop rigs or just live-lining a bunker off the structure near the river mouth and along Black Point — have connected with some real fish, mid-20s to low 30-inch range, holding deep and feeding hard once the light drops. If you've got the patience for a late trip, that's where I'd be putting my time right now, not grinding it out at noon in flat calm water with the sun beating down on a slack tide.

Bluefish have been riding those same bunker pods, and the back-bay stretch of the Niantic River has snapper blues thick enough to keep a kid entertained for an afternoon — small silver spoons or tiny bucktails under a bobber, easy action, good way to get someone hooked on this sport who isn't ready for an all-nighter chasing linesiders. Adult blues have been chopping bunker schools out toward Twotree and off Black Point in short, violent windows — nothing sustained, but when you find the birds working, it's worth a few casts of a topwater popper before they move on.

Blackfish are still off the table this month with the summer closure in effect, so don't waste drift time looking for them around Hole-in-the-Wall — that bite picks back up once the season reopens in the fall, and I'll have plenty to say about it then.

Looking ahead, the tides are about to get some muscle back. We're building toward the full moon, and that means the soft, sleepy current we've dealt with all week through Black Point and Twotree should sharpen up over the next several days. When that current strengthens, the fluke bite in the deeper channel stretches typically gets more consistent — bait gets pushed harder against structure, and the fish stack up instead of scattering. If the wind stays cooperative, I'd plan a fluke trip for later this week over an early one, timing it to hit the building tide rather than the tail end of the neap. For stripers, keep the flashlight handy and fish the dark side of the tide change around the river mouth and Black Point — that pattern isn't going anywhere as long as the bunker schools hold position and the water stays warm. Sea bass and porgies will keep producing regardless of what the current does, which makes Hole-in-the-Wall about as close to a sure thing as this beat offers right now.
